extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and legal researchers interested in U.S. censorship law, history, and media regulation
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedic summary of censorship in the United States covering legal standards, historical episodes, institutional actors (government and industry), major statutes and Supreme Court cases, and media-specific regulation. Useful as a reference/primer on what kinds of speech can be restricted and how those restrictions have been applied historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment protection against government censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Amendment protects freedom of speech and protects against government censorship; interpretation has varied and developed over time (initially applied only to the Federal government, later extended in many respects to the states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that government action to suppress speech raises First Amendment issues; historical notes about incorporation and landmark cases shape the scope of protection. Examples and related case law (Near v. Minnesota, New York Times Co. v. United States, etc.) illustrate constraints on prior restraint and other government censorship methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment does not constrain private/corporate censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Amendment protects against government censorship but not against censorship by corporations or other private entities, which are permitted to control the speech of their spokespersons, employees, or business associates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private actors may limit or punish speech through monetary loss, firing, denial of access to platforms or marketplaces; legal liability (e.g., defamation suits) and private platform policies enable non-governmental censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity is not protected speech (Miller v. California, 1973)
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Supreme Court in Miller v. California (1973) found that the First Amendment's freedom of speech does not apply to obscenity, which can therefore be censored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscenity may be regulated by government and industry; the Miller decision is the controlling precedent cited for removing constitutional protection from obscene material (the article references Miller as the basis for obscenity exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation (libel and slander) restricts speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation laws (libel and slander) limit speech; legal expenses and threat of suit can be a significant hidden restraint and produce a chilling effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that defamation suits are a common mechanism by which speech may be suppressed or chilled even where ultimate liability is uncertain; cases like New York Times Co. v. Sullivan inform standards for public-figure defamation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hate speech generally protected unless it incites illegal action
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain forms of hate speech are legal so long as they do not turn to action or incite others to commit illegal acts; more severe forms have in practice led to denial of permits or civil/legal consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes examples (denial of KKK marching permits, litigation around Westboro Baptist Church) and references how courts balance expressive content against threats, incitement, or public-safety concerns (and cites related case outcomes like Snyder v. Phelps).

rubrics_metrics.name: FCC authority to regulate 'indecent' broadcast content (time-of-day limits and fines)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Communications Commission regulates 'indecent' free-to-air broadcasting and can issue fines for airing certain profane/indecent words; it has the power to keep indecent material off the airwaves from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key cases include FCC v. Pacifica Foundation (1978) (upheld regulation of George Carlin's 'seven dirty words') and FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc. (2009) (procedural ruling on fleeting expletives). Satellite, cable, and internet outlets are not subject to the same content-based FCC regulation; fines per incident have statutory maximums (noted increases in maximum fine amounts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting vs. other media: differential regulatory treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast (over-the-air) media have historically received stricter content regulation (indecency rules) than cable, satellite, film, print, and Internet outlets, which typically enjoy greater First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court distinctions (e.g., greater regulatory power over broadcast) and examples (broadcast indecency restrictions vs. cable/internet freedoms) are used to explain why different media face different censorship regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior restraint and wartime censorship (Office of Censorship, Exec. Order 8985)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wartime and national-security contexts have supported stronger censorship powers, such as the Office of Censorship in World War II (Executive Order 8985) which authorized advance censorship of international communications and postal censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes how wartime censorship was largely accepted as constitutional in certain historical contexts, including advance review of reporters' dispatches and opening of international mail to preserve military secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comstock Law (1873) postal prohibitions on sexual/obscene materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comstock Law criminalized use of the U.S. Postal Service to send erotica, contraceptives, abortifacients, sex toys, personal letters alluding to sexual content, or information regarding those items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named for Anthony Comstock, the law exemplifies statutory censorship via postal regulation; the article lists specific categories criminalized and historical impact (book/media destruction, prosecutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedition Act / Espionage Act expansions (1917–1918)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sedition Act of 1918 (amendments to the Espionage Act of 1917) extended criminal penalties to speech that used 'disloyal, profane, scurrilous, or abusive language' about the government or interfered with war efforts; it allowed the Postmaster General to refuse delivery of such mail during wartime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute applied during declared wartime and carried imprisonment sentences; it was later repealed (December 13, 1920), but illustrates how wartime laws have restricted speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smith Act / Alien Registration Act (1940) — advocacy and membership restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Smith Act made it a criminal offense to knowingly or willfully advocate, abet, advise or teach the desirability of overthrowing the government or to organize or belong to an organization that does so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hundreds were prosecuted under the law (notably Communist Party leaders); the statute shows criminalization of certain political advocacy and was central during McCarthy-era prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immigration and Nationality (McCarran-Walter) Act — deportation/bar of suspected subversives
rubrics_metrics.description: The McCarran-Walter Act allowed the government to deport immigrants or naturalized citizens engaged in subversive activities and to bar suspected subversives from entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a tool to limit political speech/access by noncitizens and highlights immigration law as a mechanism for suppressing certain political actors or ideologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communist Control Act (1954) — civil/legal disabilities for Communist Party
rubrics_metrics.description: The Communist Control Act of 1954 declared the Communist Party and communist-infiltrated organizations 'not entitled to any of the rights, privileges, and immunities attendant upon legal bodies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents statutory efforts to deprive a political organization of normal legal protections and is cited as an example of politically motivated censorship and suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film and movie censorship history (Mutual Film v. Ohio; Joseph Burstyn 'Miracle' decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual Film (1915) held motion pictures were commerce, not art, and thus not protected by the First Amendment; Joseph Burstyn, Inc. v. Wilson (1952) overturned that, recognizing film-speech protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between those decisions local censorship boards had power to edit or ban films; the change in doctrine illustrates how constitutional protection for media has evolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedding, access agreements, and wartime press restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters embedded with military units often accept terms/restrictions on what they may report; embedded access is contingent on contracts, and wartime reporting can be limited by punishment, relocation, or dependence on military protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operational constraint functions as a form of censorship or information control even absent formal legal prohibition; the article contrasts official censorship with practical limits on reporting access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative controls on government communications and 'banned words'
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative restrictions (gag orders, review requirements, bans on particular words/terms) can limit government agency communications and scientific reporting — examples include reported bans on terms like 'global warming' or 'gender ideology' in agency communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such internal controls may not be formal statutes but have practical censorial effects (removal of web content, review of scientific publications, gag orders). The article cites examples across administrations where agencies were instructed to restrict certain terminology or release of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permits, licensing, and denial of public expression as regulatory levers
rubrics_metrics.description: Government exercise of permitting and licensing authority (e.g., marching permits, broadcast licenses, press credentials) can be used to restrict or condition expressive activities; denial or revocation can function as censorship or chilling regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include denial of marching permits to the Ku Klux Klan, threats to revoke broadcast licenses (FCC chair comments), and selective access to press events; such actions are evaluated under First Amendment standards and relevant case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry self-regulation and association rules as censorship mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry groups and private associations (e.g., National Association of Broadcasters) can adopt rules that remove controversial speakers or topics from platforms (e.g., banning 'spokesmen of controversial public issues'), effectively censoring via private-sector regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic example: Charles Coughlin was denied a license and removed from air when NAB adopted rules; industry self-regulation interacts with private-censorship doctrine and can produce de facto content control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chilling effect, legal cost, and self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonstatutory pressures — such as legal expenses, fear of litigation, loss of employment, or market sanctions — create a chilling effect leading individuals and outlets to self-censor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that beyond explicit legal prohibitions, economic and reputational risks (lawsuits, funding bans, deplatforming) are powerful restraints on speech and can be exercised by both state and private actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landmark Supreme Court cases and legal doctrines shaping censorship boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of Supreme Court decisions and legal doctrines define limits and exceptions to free speech (e.g., Near v. Minnesota on prior restraint; New York Times Co. v. Sullivan on defamation; FCC v. Pacifica on broadcast indecency; Snyder v. Phelps on protest/speech limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These precedents are the primary legal yardsticks for evaluating whether particular restrictions or censorship actions are constitutional; the article lists many relevant cases and doctrinal touchstones.
